值得閱讀的理由

  • 破解「高收入必然等於高財富」的普遍迷思，清楚剖析收支管理與財務智商對終身資產的決定性影響。
  • 劃分25至55歲黃金三十年的職涯與財富階段，為不同年齡層提供清晰的資產累積策略與進階路徑。
  • 梳理財商層級的思維轉變，指導如何跳脫單純儲蓄與賺取短期價差的陷阱，邁向長期複利與現金流建構。

摘要

高收入不等於高財富：財務智商決定最終資產

作者從自身涉足房地產並走過人生低谷的經歷切入，強調賺錢能力不等於累積財富的能力。許多人認為年薪三百萬的人二十年後必定比年薪一百五十萬的人更有錢，但作者指出，若缺乏良好的花費習慣與理財紀律，高收入者可能因龐大開銷而剩餘無幾；反觀收入較低但能持續節約並長期投資的人，累積的資產反而更為可觀。兩者之間的關鍵分水嶺在於財務智商（FQ），唯有全面理解金錢、負債與現金流的本質，才能徹底扭轉財富格局。

人生黃金三十年：從技能勞力走向資本運作

作者將25歲至55歲的奮鬥歷程拆解為三大發展階段：在25至35歲的第一階段，主要仰賴個人勞力、體力與專業技能賺取第一桶金；進入35至45歲的第二階段，則轉為依靠經驗、人脈網絡與專業聲譽來快速擴張財富；到了45至55歲的第三階段，核心則完全轉向依賴「錢滾錢」、資訊差與精準投資來獲利。釐清這三個階段的定位，有助於在不同的年齡階段做出最適合的資產布局決策。

進階財商思維：從單純儲蓄到打造長期現金流

作者進一步剖析財商的前幾個層級：第一層是門檻最低卻最脆弱的單純儲蓄者，極易遭到通貨膨脹蠶食購買力；第二層是追逐買低賣高的賺價差者，因難以永不犯錯且耗費心力，本質上如同另一份全職工作；第三層是懂得善用時間複利與長期投資的人，特別適合本金不多但擁有時間優勢的年輕人；而邁入第四層則是學習像玩大富翁遊戲般建構被動現金流，透過持有能夠持續產出收入的資產，讓財富積累走向穩定而永續的良性循環。

If we put ourselves in the bank’s position when evaluating a business—for example, if I get an order and need 10 million for supplies, with a potential revenue of 50 million, but I only have 2 million in cash—then I would borrow 8 million from the bank to secure that 50 million. order. I already knew I’d have these returns for the year, so I used the bank’s lower interest rate to leverage. I did this because I couldn't manage a 50-million-dollar business alone, but with the bank, we could do it together. Of course, business always carries risks ; there is no 100%guarantee. Every endeavor, every bit of wealth accumulated, and every choice comes with a different price. The rewards can be great, but the costs are usually just as high. So, everyone needs to realize one thing: debt is not wealth; debt is a tool that must be managed. Next, we. reach the seventh level. Why do I say buy houses and never sell them? I’m not sure if I’ve said this in public, but the rule is to buy and never sell. For example, 10 years ago, I bought a house for 290,000 per ping, and now it’s up to 600,000 or 700,000. Why wouldn’t I sell it? Wouldn’t I make a huge profit? Because for buying houses, the bank covers 80%, so we only put up 20%of the capital. Calculating that, it could be a return on investment of several hundred or even a thousand percent. But why do we say never sell? This is where it gets interesting. Let’s use an example. Suppose I buy a house today for 30 million. A few years later, it appreciates to 50 million. So, what’s. the difference? The difference is 20 million. The conventional way of thinking is that if I sell the house, I make 20 million. But my first question would be: has the condition of this house changed? Does it still have room for growth? Is this area stable? Are the rental yields good? Is the local population still increasing? If it’s such a great asset, why would I want to sell it? Isn’t it a golden goose? This is when we can start looking into something else called "refinancing." Suppose the house is now worth 50 million, whether by official assessment , bank valuation, or actual transaction. records. Assuming we bought it for 30 million, how much could we borrow? At 80 %, you could borrow 24 million. Now, at 50 million, you can borrow 40 million! 40 million minus 24 million, you get an extra 16 million! You can take out those 16 million to reinvest, making even better investments. My original asset hasn’t disappeared; if I rent it out, it continues to generate rental income, which can cover the monthly loan payments I was already making. Let’s not use houses as an example. I don’t want to keep using real estate, especially with the current market crackdown. If I take 16 million.

to buy TSMC, or put 50 percent into MediaTek, it could generate incredible returns, instantly multiplying that 16 million. Even catching Bitcoin or the right currency at the right time—the opportunities are endless. I have the choice to do this or not. Since I already hold the leverage, I can choose to pull that money out, or I can choose not to. I’d only pull it out for a business or investment I’m highly confident in. Even if it doesn’t go as planned—say we just break even and the 16 million earns. nothing—I can just put it back in the bank. My asset remains unchanged; the house is still valuable. A house that has risen to 50 million generates different rental yields compared to when it was 30 million five years or ten years ago. The prerequisite for all this is having enough cash flow and emergency funds to handle potential investment failures. It’s about controlling your risk. If you over-leverage yourself, taking out a 70 percent loan, I think that’s. very dangerous. To complete this concept: good assets should be held long-term, but sound financial decisions must never ignore risk. That is the core of what I mean by "buy and never sell." Discussing the seventh level brought about a clash of ideas. Now, entering the eighth level, I’ve found my way of thinking has shifted again. Before, we talked about which stock is better, which house is worth buying, or which product has higher returns. But at this stage, we no longer care about single investments; we care about the entire balance sheet of. our family or company. Let’s assume someone has 1 billion in assets: 300 million in real estate, 200 million in land, 150 million in stocks and ETFs, 100 million in corporate equity, 100 million in USD fixed-income assets, and 50 million in cash. This is just an example; we cannot say this is an ideal investment allocation. It sounds extremely wealthy—obviously, with 1 billion, they are rich. Many people would think, "If I had 1 billion, I'd retire, why would I be watching your YouTube channel?" However, at this point , we need to consider a few questions. In this situation, how much debt does this person have? Second, how much interest must be paid annually? Third,. how many assets can be quickly liquidated? That is to say, we look at asset liquidity. Real estate is an asset with very low liquidity, while stocks and cryptocurrencies are assets with very high liquidity. Next, the fourth question: How much cash flow does this person have? Fifth: If real estate prices drop by 20%, will there be capital pressure? Sixth: If the business suddenly runs into trouble, is there enough liquid capital to cover it? You will find that just looking at 1 billion in total assets cannot determine if their financial situation is healthy. If they have 800 million in debt and most of their assets are illiquid, the risk could be extremely high. Conversely, if. someone only has 300 million in assets, but their debt ratio is low, cash flow is stable, and they hold sufficient liquid funds, then their financial security is clearly better. So, at this level, what is it that we truly need to manage? It still comes down to the word "assets." At this point, it’s no longer just about investing; it’s about asset management and asset allocation. Now, moving to the ninth layer: Why does true wealth require global allocation? For my first 20 years in real estate, I only focused on domestic property. I hadn't stepped out into the world. The world’s wealthiest people, multinational. corporations, and global tycoons are all highly international. So, after I started dealing with international real estate, my perspective broadened. I’ve learned much more from seniors and mentors about their views on global positioning and international perspectives. I used to focus solely on Taiwan, because I thought Taiwanese real estate was great and our social media presence was good too. But staying stuck in our own echo chamber makes it very difficult for us to lead our companies and businesses to break through to the next level. Once we were exposed to international real estate, we started to learn about global asset allocation. Of course, we have met many clients, and.

these clients naturally have assets that are many times larger. Let me ask you a question: suppose you have a hospital, houses in Taiwan, stocks, bank savings, insurance, funds, and even USD fixed deposits and policies—do you think you have effectively diversified your risks ? Many people say, "Yes, I have some money in liquid assets and some in non-liquid ones, and I didn't just buy real estate." But let me tell you, we should consider one more thing: all these assets are currently concentrated in Taiwan, rely primarily on the New Taiwan Dollar, and exist within the same financial and legal environment. Taiwan cannot connect with many places, and, of. course, the situation across the Taiwan Strait is even more complex. Although many people will say, "I have already diversified my risks because I have put my assets into different categories." But, they are all in the same financial environment, denominated in the same currency. Even if we buy a USD fixed deposit at any financial institution in Taiwan, we are still using NTD and relying on local financial institutions . Our focus is on global layout. There is nothing wrong with doing these things in Taiwan—the things mentioned in the previous points are fine. It is just that we have reached a different level now, which requires a different perspective. That is why I believe that. when a person’s assets reach a certain level, they should start studying global allocation. Global allocation is not just for the wealthy; even if we only have a few tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands. You can study global stocks or other international assets through suitable and legal investment channels. The difference is just that the larger your asset scale, the more issues you need to handle. I would suggest buying things like USD assets, but why do I think the US dollar is worth studying? Because the US dollar plays a very important role in global trade, international finance, as well as the pricing of crude oil and gold, and in many cross-border transactions. If all your wealth is in New Taiwan Dollars , then holding some US dollar assets may. help diversify the risk of a single currency. So I want to specifically remind you that the US dollar is not immune to depreciation, and US dollar assets are not immune to losses. If you hold US dollars, you still have to face exchange rates, interest rates, and inflation. As long as you print money, you will still have these problems. What is truly important is not to tell everyone to convert all their money into US dollar assets or foreign assets, but to ensure our assets are not overly dependent on a single currency. Next is real estate investment. We have been investing in real estate ourselves over the past two years. This is what I always tell everyone: we will only share what we are doing ourselves, which of course includes cryptocurrency. We hold cryptocurrency ourselves, and my returns on cryptocurrency have actually been. very impressive. Also, regarding real estate, its pricing unit is the dirham, which is long-term pegged to the US dollar. Its exchange rate path is completely synchronized. Global real estate, beyond the investment characteristics of the property itself, also involves allocation across different currencies and jurisdictions. Furthermore, overseas real estate is not without risk. You still need to study supply and demand, rental yields, developer credibility, transaction costs , regulations, and future liquidity. You cannot assume it is safer just because it is overseas. There are many countries for overseas real estate. We have traveled to Thailand, Japan, Korea, and many places in Southeast Asia, and even Australia, the UK, and the US. We have been to all these places, but I haven't invested everywhere. Of course, I only. promote what I have researched myself. Next, I'll talk about some other tools, specifically the planning I’ve been doing for international insurance policies. Just as Taiwan has its own policies, there are international policies as well. By flying to different countries, we can see that different nations have different products. As the saying goes, there is no harm without comparison. Many things can still be used anywhere, especially some offshore insurance products, which are tax-exempt and convenient. The functions of trusts —whether you want to pass on assets or divide them—are very powerful. They can even allow for transfers without incurring any taxes. Many people have heard of Hong Kong, but of course, Singapore has them too, Dubai has its own, we have them in the UAE, and there. are even options in Bermuda. I think these options can be described as diverse and varied, but I must say upfront: there is no such thing as getting rich overnight. When talking about offshore financial products, not everything can be marketed in Taiwan. It’s like buying medicine: what’s allowed abroad might not be in Taiwan. Everyone should be mindful of legality when accumulating and creating assets. The second type is cryptocurrency assets . Personally, I find blockchain technology to be a world that is very difficult to enter. Blockchain technology combines many things like semiconductors and AI, but just the same , cryptocurrency remains a gray area in Taiwan. Take Bitcoin for example. Bitcoin has varied perceptions; some see.

it as a high-risk investment tool, while others view it as a digital asset with scarcity. However, its price is highly volatile and it trades 24/7 without stopping, so you could wake up in the middle of the night and place an order. But let me be clear, I am not telling everyone to do this. This is just my observation in this area. Of course, there are also stablecoins like USDT, which is pegged to the US dollar. It is already circulating in many places around the world, and we can even use USDT directly to purchase overseas real estate in Dubai. While stablecoins aim to maintain a relatively stable value. pegged to a specific fiat currency, there are risks regarding the issuer's reserve assets, potential de-pegging, and exchange custody and regulation. Therefore, I believe a truly mature investor doesn't reject all cryptocurrencies at the sound of them, nor does one want to go all-in just because they heard someone made money. Instead, you should understand what role it can play in your overall asset allocation and how much risk you can personally tolerate. Let’s summarize the concept here: global asset allocation doesn't necessarily mean we must buy overseas real estate, offshore insurance policies, or cryptocurrencies; it means starting to learn to examine our own wealth from different perspectives. The world is huge, but like I used to be, I was really just stuck in Taiwan. Which. countries should my assets be concentrated in? Which currency risks can I bear? Which banks or financial institutions do I rely on? Can my assets be liquidated smoothly? And even, if one day I want to pass my wealth to my family or children, how can I let them receive it legally and smoothly? Of course, we also want to avoid incurring huge tax liabilities. These questions are exactly why global asset allocation is so important. Speaking of this, let’s talk about the tenth level: evolving from owning assets to controlling capital. That’s not something I’ll easily encounter in my lifetime. When your assets reach a certain level, you have to face a different tier of problems; it’s no longer just about how. to earn more money. Instead, it’s about how to protect this wealth, how to manage assets across different countries , and even how to arrange for the next generation's inheritance. It's about preventing assets from being impacted by a family member, a business issue, or a legal dispute, and avoiding the freezing of assets due to poor management. So, at this stage, we start exploring tools we weren't familiar with before, such as holding companies, or special purpose vehicles, known as SPVs, and trusts, which I’ve encountered but found quite complex to implement. "Family office" is a term mentioned so often, but I don't think it's for everyone; very few people actually need one. The truth is, the. purpose of these tools isn't to chase the highest return on investment, but to clearly define the ownership, management , control, and beneficiary rights of assets. Of course, many of these structures are very sophisticated. Setting one up doesn't automatically mean you are exempt from taxes, nor does setting up a trust mean your property is completely shielded from legal issues or creditors. Different countries have different regulations regarding tax residency, ultimate beneficial owners, overseas income, inheritance, and anti-tax evasion. Therefore, true high-level wealth planning must be built on a foundation that is legal, transparent, and sustainable. I want to share a concept here: tax planning is not tax evasion, and asset planning is. not about hiding wealth. It must be legal. Those who have attended our presentations know that we place great importance on being legal, compliant, and paying taxes reasonably. For the past five years, we have had PwC handle our financial and tax audits, so I have certainly paid plenty of tuition and taxes in this area. Therefore, truly valuable planning is about making asset holding and operational risk management more efficient within the bounds of the law. I believe that when a person starts to think about these issues, they have already begun to transition from a simple investor toward an asset manager , or even...A capital manager. This is what I call the tenth level. I also aspire to reach this level, but I feel I. am still quite far off. Some people might think, why worry so much? Doesn't all this have nothing to do with me? I only earn a monthly income of 35,000 or 40,000. The more that happens, the more I want to tell everyone that it actually matters a lot, because financial literacy isn't something we wait to learn only after we're rich. You don't need to be rich yet, but you need a wealthy mindset first. We must build the right financial concepts so that when the money comes, we can hold onto it and even multiply it. If you're just starting out and your income isn't high yet, I suggest focusing on three things first. First, increase your earning power—work two jobs to build capital quickly. Second, control your living.

costs and build an emergency fund. I think this is the hardest part because social media is so tempting, making self-discipline very difficult. If you've worked for 10 years and built up some capital, you can start researching cash flow. This could be real estate, asset allocation, studying stocks, or cryptocurrency, but never rush to get rich by taking on leverage you can't handle. If you have already accumulated tens of millions or more, I think you should more thoroughly examine your balance sheet instead of just looking at how much you earned this year. I am learning myself, and I think it's great , but I've always felt that learning and. performing well are two different things . There’s so much practical experience involved; wealth isn't determined by a single investment, but by the accumulation of correct long-term decisions. Finally, I want to share a concept I've come to agree with more and more: when we are young, we easily make making money our primary goal. I remember when I was a fresh graduate, I told myself, "You need to earn a million ." But as we start to meet people at different levels, we realize that what's truly worth pursuing might not be the income figure itself, but whether we can possess the right to choose our lifestyle. Strictly speaking, I don't have it either. I often have to work, and I also want to spend time with my. kids, but it's okay, let's encourage each other. Keep working hard. Lastly, to those who watched until here, if you're interested, I’m planning a small gathering to share what I actually do, like my investments in Linkou real estate or some of my offshore financial products and policies. Would you be interested in that? I have a lot of insights on this, so if you'd like to explore these topics, let's first see how many people are interested in signing up. We'll post a Google Form here; if you'd like to participate, you can sign up and select the topics you're more interested in. We'll group people with similar interests together for these small gatherings. I can tell you exactly what I'm working on, but I won't go into detail in a public video. That's. all for today's show. I hope this episode is helpful to many of you. Finally, I wish you all a fantastic cash flow, and hope you can all manage your wealth and assets well, giving yourselves more freedom and choices in life. That's it for our show today. If you enjoyed our program, remember to hit like, share, subscribe, and follow us.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 破解「高收入必然等於高財富」的普遍迷思，清楚剖析收支管理與財務智商對終身資產的決定性影響。
  • 劃分25至55歲黃金三十年的職涯與財富階段，為不同年齡層提供清晰的資產累積策略與進階路徑。
  • 梳理財商層級的思維轉變，指導如何跳脫單純儲蓄與賺取短期價差的陷阱，邁向長期複利與現金流建構。

摘要

高收入不等於高財富：財務智商決定最終資產

作者從自身涉足房地產並走過人生低谷的經歷切入，強調賺錢能力不等於累積財富的能力。許多人認為年薪三百萬的人二十年後必定比年薪一百五十萬的人更有錢，但作者指出，若缺乏良好的花費習慣與理財紀律，高收入者可能因龐大開銷而剩餘無幾；反觀收入較低但能持續節約並長期投資的人，累積的資產反而更為可觀。兩者之間的關鍵分水嶺在於財務智商（FQ），唯有全面理解金錢、負債與現金流的本質，才能徹底扭轉財富格局。

人生黃金三十年：從技能勞力走向資本運作

作者將25歲至55歲的奮鬥歷程拆解為三大發展階段：在25至35歲的第一階段，主要仰賴個人勞力、體力與專業技能賺取第一桶金；進入35至45歲的第二階段，則轉為依靠經驗、人脈網絡與專業聲譽來快速擴張財富；到了45至55歲的第三階段，核心則完全轉向依賴「錢滾錢」、資訊差與精準投資來獲利。釐清這三個階段的定位，有助於在不同的年齡階段做出最適合的資產布局決策。

進階財商思維：從單純儲蓄到打造長期現金流

作者進一步剖析財商的前幾個層級：第一層是門檻最低卻最脆弱的單純儲蓄者，極易遭到通貨膨脹蠶食購買力；第二層是追逐買低賣高的賺價差者，因難以永不犯錯且耗費心力，本質上如同另一份全職工作；第三層是懂得善用時間複利與長期投資的人，特別適合本金不多但擁有時間優勢的年輕人；而邁入第四層則是學習像玩大富翁遊戲般建構被動現金流，透過持有能夠持續產出收入的資產，讓財富積累走向穩定而永續的良性循環。

================================================

The ability to earn an income is not the same as the ability to accumulate wealth . When our understanding of money, assets, liabilities, and cash flow becomes more complete, our perspective on wealth changes entirely. Debt itself is a very powerful wealth tool; debt is not wealth, but a tool that needs to be managed. If you are interested, we can host a small gathering where I can share how I put these into practice. Hello, everyone. Welcome to "Property Talk." Today on Property Talk, I’d like to share my secrets to wealth. You might think that since we work in real estate , we’ve made some money from it, but I believe that is still a long way from. being personally wealthy. I am 40 years old, and I’ve had many seniors and mentors teaching me. I didn't just know this overnight; I went through many pitfalls and took many hard knocks. If you’ve seen my other videos or interviews on other channels, you know I hit rock bottom before slowly climbing back up. In terms of wealth, there are so many people richer than us. The wealth gap is extreme—scarily so—and there are more and more wealthy people in Taiwan. As someone who started from scratch and took many detours, I hope to share knowledge that I truly find useful with those who might need it. If you are already much wealthier than us, then. this video might not be very useful to you, but that’s okay; I still want to share it with those who need it. Let me first ask everyone a question: If there are two people, one with an annual salary of 3 million and the other with only 1.5 million, who do you think will be wealthier in 10 or 20 years? Most people would naturally think the one earning 3 million a year will be wealthier. You can't say they are wrong , but you can't say they are entirely right either. Although there is a gap in the wealth we acquire, spending habits and financial management habits will have a far greater impact on our ultimate financial outcome.
